question: What is the time complexity of common Python built-in operations like list append, dict lookup, and set membership?
title: Big-O for Python Built-in Operations
direct_answer: List append is O(1) amortized (O(n) occasional resize). List insert at index 0 is O(n). Dict lookup, set membership, and dict/set insertion are O(1) average (O(n) worst case hash collision). List membership (in) is O(n). Sorted list binary search (bisect) is O(log n). Knowing these matters because nested loops with list membership checks that could be sets is a very common O(n²) bug.
interviewer_intent: Tests whether the candidate thinks about performance in Python's specific data structures, not just abstract algorithmic complexity.

sections.title: Python built-in complexity reference
sections.content:
Python's collections have specific performance characteristics that differ from their conceptual equivalents. The most important ones to know cold:

list: append O(1) amortized (Python over-allocates; occasional resize is O(n) but amortized across N appends is O(1)). insert(0, x) is O(n) — everything shifts. pop() from end is O(1). pop(0) or pop(i) is O(n). Membership 'in' is O(n) linear scan. Sorting is O(n log n) (Timsort).

dict: get, set, delete, 'in' are all O(1) average. O(n) worst case if all keys hash to the same bucket (extremely rare with Python's modern hash randomization). As of Python 3.7+, dicts preserve insertion order.

set: 'in', add, remove are O(1) average. Union/intersection are O(min(len(s1), len(s2))) to O(len(s1) + len(s2)) depending on operation. Converting a list to a set to do membership lookups is the classic O(n) → O(1) optimization.

collections.deque: appendleft and popleft are O(1). List.insert(0) and list.pop(0) are O(n).

sections.title: The common O(n²) bug and fix
sections.content:
# O(n²) — list 'in' is O(n), done n times
def has_duplicates_slow(lst):
    seen = []
    for item in lst:
        if item in seen:    # O(n) scan every time
            return True
        seen.append(item)
    return False

# O(n) — set 'in' is O(1)
def has_duplicates_fast(lst):
    seen = set()
    for item in lst:
        if item in seen:    # O(1) hash lookup
            return True
        seen.add(item)
    return False

# Even simpler
def has_duplicates(lst):
    return len(lst) != len(set(lst))

# O(n²) API endpoint bug
# items is a list, valid_ids is a list — 'in' is O(n)
valid_ids = [1, 2, 3, ...]   # 10,000 items
result = [item for item in items if item.id in valid_ids]  # O(n*m)

# Fix: convert once to set
valid_set = set(valid_ids)   # O(n) once
result = [item for item in items if item.id in valid_set]  # O(n)

sections.title: Complexity rules to know cold
items: list 'in' is O(n) — always convert to set for repeated membership tests
dict/set lookup is O(1) average — the fundamental reason dicts are everywhere
list.insert(0) and list.pop(0) are O(n) — use deque for queues
list.append is O(1) amortized — safe for growing lists
sorted() is O(n log n) Timsort — faster for partially sorted data

seo.metaTitle: Python Big-O Complexity — List, Dict, Set Operations
seo.metaDescription: Time complexity reference for Python built-in operations: list append O(1), dict lookup O(1), set membership O(1). Includes common O(n²) bugs and fixes.

speakable_v2.hook: The most common interview performance bug: list 'in' in a loop — it's O(n²) that looks like it should be fast.

beats.content: List membership check 'in' is O(n) — Python scans every element. Dict and set membership is O(1) hash lookup. That's the most important complexity difference in day-to-day Python.
If you're checking 'if x in my_list' inside a loop over n items, you've got O(n²). Convert the list to a set once before the loop — same O(n) setup cost but now each check is O(1).
For queues, use collections.deque not list. list.pop(0) shifts every element — O(n). deque.popleft() is O(1).

speakable_v2.cap: The two rules that fix 80% of Python performance bugs: use sets for membership tests, use deque for queues.
speakable_v2.followup_handoff: Follow up with heapq for priority queues or bisect for sorted list binary search.
